subject: geography
topicDisplay: The Changing Landscapes of the UK
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Where are most of the UK's upland areas located?
options: Evenly spread across the whole country
questions.explain: The UK's upland areas are concentrated in the north and west, where older, more resistant rocks are found.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of an igneous rock found in the UK?
questions.explain: Granite is an igneous rock formed from cooled magma and forms resistant upland areas such as Dartmoor.

questions.q: Why do upland landscapes tend to form in areas of igneous and metamorphic rock?
options: These rocks are hard and resistant to erosion
These rocks are soft and easily weathered
These rocks are always found near the sea
These rocks contain large amounts of water
questions.explain: Igneous and metamorphic rocks are hard and resistant, so they are worn down slowly and remain as high upland areas.

questions.q: Why are lowland landscapes common in the south and east of the UK?
options: They are underlain by younger, softer sedimentary rocks
They are underlain by hard igneous rocks
They receive the highest rainfall in the UK
They have never been affected by weathering
questions.explain: The south and east are dominated by younger, softer sedimentary rocks such as clay and chalk, which erode more easily to form lowlands.

questions.q: What is hydraulic action?
options: The force of waves compressing air into cracks in the rock
Rocks grinding against each other and becoming smaller
Sand and pebbles scraping against the cliff
questions.explain: Hydraulic action is the erosive force of water and compressed air being forced into cracks, weakening and breaking the rock.

questions.q: Which coastal erosion process involves rocks and pebbles colliding and gradually becoming smaller and rounder?
questions.explain: Attrition is where transported rocks knock against one another, becoming smaller, smoother and more rounded over time.

questions.q: Which statement best describes destructive waves?
options: They have a strong backwash that removes material and erodes the coast
They have a strong swash that builds up beaches
They only occur in calm weather
They deposit large amounts of sediment
questions.explain: Destructive waves have a weak swash but a strong backwash, so they remove sediment and erode the coastline.

questions.q: A headland shows a wave-cut cave that has widened over time. What is the correct sequence of landforms that follows as erosion continues?
questions.explain: Erosion enlarges a cave into an arch, which collapses to leave a stack, later eroded down to a stump.

questions.q: In longshore drift, in which direction does the backwash carry material down the beach?
options: Straight back down at right angles to the coastline
At an angle following the prevailing wind
Up the beach towards the land
questions.explain: Swash moves material up the beach at the angle of the prevailing wind, but backwash returns it straight down at right angles under gravity, creating a zig-zag movement.

questions.q: How does a spit form along a coastline?
options: Longshore drift deposits material where the coastline changes direction
Waves erode a headland into an arch
A river deposits sediment across its mouth
Freeze-thaw weathering breaks down a cliff
questions.explain: A spit forms when longshore drift continues to deposit sediment out into the sea where the coast changes direction, forming a ridge of material.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of hard engineering coastal management?
questions.explain: Groynes are a hard engineering method that trap sediment moved by longshore drift to build up the beach.

questions.q: What does the coastal management strategy of managed retreat (coastal realignment) involve?
options: Allowing low-value land to flood and the coastline to move inland
Building a large concrete sea wall along the whole coast
Adding sand to widen an eroding beach
Placing large boulders at the base of a cliff
questions.explain: Managed retreat allows low-value land to flood naturally, creating habitats and reducing the cost and energy of the sea reaching valued areas.

questions.q: A coastal town wants to protect a busy seafront promenade from powerful destructive waves while keeping a walkway. Which method is most suitable?
questions.explain: A sea wall reflects wave energy and protects built-up land while providing a walkway, making it suitable for a valuable seafront.

questions.q: Which type of erosion dominates in the upper course of a river, deepening the channel?
questions.explain: In the upper course the river cuts downwards through vertical erosion, creating steep, narrow V-shaped valleys.

questions.q: In which course of a river are waterfalls and gorges typically found?
questions.explain: Waterfalls and the gorges left by their retreat are typical features of the upper course where vertical erosion is strong.

questions.q: In a meander, where does the greatest erosion occur?
options: On the outer bank, where water flows fastest
On the inner bank, where water flows slowest
In the centre of the channel only
questions.explain: Faster flow on the outer bank causes erosion and a river cliff, while slower flow on the inner bank deposits sediment as a slip-off slope.

questions.q: A meander becomes so pronounced that its neck is eroded through, leaving a curved body of water cut off from the main channel. What has formed?
questions.explain: When erosion breaks through the narrow neck of a meander, the river takes the straighter route and deposition cuts off the loop, forming an ox-bow lake.

questions.q: Where along a river are natural levées most likely to form?
options: On the floodplain in the lower course
At the source of the river
questions.explain: Levées are raised banks formed by repeated deposition during floods on the floodplain of the lower course.

questions.q: Why do wide, flat floodplains develop in the lower course of a river?
options: Lateral erosion and deposition during floods spread sediment across the valley floor
Vertical erosion cuts a deep narrow gorge
Freeze-thaw weathering breaks up the valley sides
The river only transports material and never deposits it
questions.explain: In the lower course, lateral erosion widens the valley and floods deposit alluvium, building a broad, flat floodplain.

questions.q: A river authority wants to store water and control the discharge released downstream to reduce flooding. Which hard engineering strategy fits this aim?
questions.explain: A dam holds water in a reservoir so that discharge can be controlled and released steadily, reducing flood risk downstream.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel GCSE Geography B (1GB0) specification; The Changing Landscapes of the UK
